questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man with a known mitral valve abnormality presents with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, fatigue, and night sweats. Two months ago he had a tooth extraction. A new murmur is heard. Three sets of blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase negative, produce partial (alpha) hemolysis on blood agar, and grow up to the optochin disk without a zone of inhibition.

Which property of this organism best explains its ability to colonize the damaged valve?
choices: Synthesis of dextrans from glucose that bind fibrin-platelet aggregates
A polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis in the bloodstream
Superantigen release that activates large numbers of T cells nonspecifically
Coagulase production that converts fibrinogen to a protective fibrin coat
Biofilm slime made of polysaccharide intercellular adhesin on devices
questions.note:
**Viridans streptococci cause subacute endocarditis on damaged valves after dental procedures because their dextrans bind fibrin-platelet aggregates.**

Alpha-hemolytic, catalase-negative streptococci in chains that are optochin resistant belong to the viridans group (for example S. mutans and S. mitis), which live in the mouth. A dental extraction lets them into the bloodstream, and a subacute course on an abnormal valve is their classic picture.

Viridans streptococci make dextrans from glucose. Dextran lets them stick to the fibrin-platelet aggregates that build up on damaged valves, which is why they are the most common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis after dental work.

Synthesis of dextrans from glucose that bind fibrin-platelet aggregates: correct. Dextran synthesis lets viridans streptococci adhere to fibrin-platelet clots on damaged valves.

A polysaccharide capsule that blocks phagocytosis in the bloodstream: incorrect. An essential polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence factor of S. pneumoniae, which is optochin sensitive.

Superantigen release that activates large numbers of T cells nonspecifically: incorrect. Superantigens (SpeA, SpeB, TSST-1) belong to S. pyogenes and S. aureus and cause toxic shock, not valve adherence.

Coagulase production that converts fibrinogen to a protective fibrin coat: incorrect. Coagulase is a feature of S. aureus, a catalase-positive cluster-forming coccus.

Biofilm slime made of polysaccharide intercellular adhesin on devices: incorrect. Polysaccharide intercellular adhesin is the biofilm slime of S. epidermidis on catheters and prostheses.

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman in the intensive care unit for 3 weeks develops fever and a urinary tract infection while on an indwelling catheter. The urine grows catalase-negative, oxidase-negative Gram-positive cocci that are non-hemolytic, grow in 6.5% NaCl, tolerate bile, and do not grow on mannitol salt agar. The isolate is resistant to vancomycin.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
choices: Enterococcus faecalis
Streptococcus bovis group
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Enterococcus faecium
Streptococcus agalactiae
questions.note:
**Enterococci grow in 6.5% NaCl and bile; E. faecium does not grow on mannitol salt agar and is usually the vancomycin-resistant species.**

Growth in 6.5% NaCl and bile tolerance identify an enterococcus, a hardy gut organism that persists on hospital surfaces and causes catheter-associated urinary infections, peritonitis, wound infections, and bacteremia.

The two human species are told apart here by mannitol salt agar, on which E. faecalis grows and E. faecium does not, and by vancomycin. E. faecalis is more common overall, but E. faecium is usually the vancomycin-resistant species (VRE) and is one of the ESKAPE pathogens.

Enterococcus faecalis: incorrect. E. faecalis grows on mannitol salt agar and is less often vancomycin resistant.

Streptococcus bovis group: incorrect. S. bovis group does not grow in 6.5% NaCl.

Staphylococcus saprophyticus: incorrect. S. saprophyticus is a catalase-positive staphylococcus that causes urinary infections in young women.

Enterococcus faecium: correct. A salt-tolerant enterococcus that fails on mannitol salt agar and resists vancomycin is E. faecium.

Streptococcus agalactiae: incorrect. S. agalactiae is beta hemolytic and does not grow in 6.5% NaCl.

questions.stem:
Two urine isolates from different patients are both motile, oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rods that swarm on agar, produce hydrogen sulfide, and are urease positive. Isolate 1 is from a previously healthy outpatient with cystitis and is indole negative. Isolate 2 is from a patient on chemotherapy with a wound infection and is indole positive.

Which statement about these two isolates is correct?
choices: Isolate 1 is P. vulgaris, the usual cause of community cystitis
Isolate 2 is P. mirabilis, which typically spares healthy hosts
Isolate 1 is P. mirabilis and is usually sensitive to ampicillin
Both isolates are Salmonella serovars separated by indole
Indole production distinguishes Proteus from Pseudomonas species
questions.note:
**Among swarming, urease-positive Proteus species, indole production identifies P. vulgaris and separates it from the common urinary pathogen P. mirabilis.**

Swarming motility, hydrogen sulfide and urease place both isolates in the genus Proteus. Indole is the test the lecture uses to separate the two species: P. vulgaris produces indole and P. mirabilis does not.

P. mirabilis is the second most common bacterial cause of urinary tract infection and is usually sensitive to ampicillin and cephalosporins, while P. vulgaris is isolated less often, generally infects immunosuppressed patients, and is not reliably sensitive to those drugs.

Isolate 1 is P. vulgaris, the usual cause of community cystitis: incorrect. P. vulgaris is indole positive and is not the usual community urinary pathogen.

Isolate 2 is P. mirabilis, which typically spares healthy hosts: incorrect. P. mirabilis is indole negative and commonly infects otherwise healthy people.

Isolate 1 is P. mirabilis and is usually sensitive to ampicillin: correct. The indole-negative isolate is P. mirabilis, usually sensitive to ampicillin and cephalosporins.

Both isolates are Salmonella serovars separated by indole: incorrect. Salmonella makes hydrogen sulfide but does not swarm and is urease negative.

Indole production distinguishes Proteus from Pseudomonas species: incorrect. Pseudomonas is oxidase positive, so oxidase, not indole, separates it from Proteus.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man has nausea and vomiting followed by cramping and diarrhea that began about 36 hours after a picnic where undercooked chicken and a homemade egg dish were served. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F). Stool culture on Hektoen enteric agar yields black-centered colonies. The isolate is motile, oxidase negative, and does not ferment lactose.

Which laboratory feature identified on this plate best separates this organism from Shigella?
choices: Hydrogen sulfide production
Oxidase activity
Lactose fermentation
Growth in 6.5% salt
Urease production
questions.note:
**Salmonella is motile and produces hydrogen sulfide (black colonies on Hektoen agar), which separates it from non-motile, hydrogen sulfide-negative Shigella.**

Poultry and eggs, an incubation of roughly 24 to 48 hours, and fever with cramping diarrhea fit Salmonella gastroenteritis. Both Salmonella and Shigella are non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rods, so those features cannot separate them.

Salmonella produces hydrogen sulfide, which precipitates as black colonies on Hektoen enteric agar, and it is motile. Shigella makes no hydrogen sulfide and is non-motile. Most Salmonella gastroenteritis is treated supportively.

**Salmonella | Shigella**

- Motility: Motile; Non-motile
- Hydrogen sulfide: Produced; Not produced
- Lactose: Not fermented; Not fermented

Hydrogen sulfide production: correct. Hydrogen sulfide, seen as black colonies, separates Salmonella from Shigella.

Oxidase activity: incorrect. Both organisms are oxidase negative, so this does not distinguish them.

Lactose fermentation: incorrect. Neither organism ferments lactose.

Growth in 6.5% salt: incorrect. Salt tolerance is used for enterococci, not for enteric Gram-negative rods.

Urease production: incorrect. Urease is a feature of Proteus and Helicobacter, not of Salmonella.

questions.stem:
Respiratory epithelium is infected in vitro with a small, cell wall-free bacterium that attaches to cilia and microvilli by a terminal organelle. Over the next day the ciliated cells stop beating, the nuclei show vacuolization, and the epithelial layer sheds into the medium. The effect is reproduced by adding a purified ADP-ribosylating protein from the organism to uninfected cells.

This purified protein is best described as the cause of which clinical picture?
choices: Massive watery diarrhea with fluid and electrolyte loss
Spastic paralysis beginning in the masseter muscles
A necrotic black skin lesion at the inoculation site
Pseudomembrane formation over the tonsils and pharynx
Persistent cough with inflammation and airway dysfunction
questions.note:
**Mycoplasma pneumoniae produces the ADP-ribosylating CARDS toxin, which damages ciliated respiratory epithelium and causes cough and airway dysfunction.**

A small bacterium without a cell wall that attaches to cilia through a terminal organelle is Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and its ADP-ribosylating toxin is the community-acquired respiratory distress syndrome (CARDS) toxin.

CARDS toxin interferes with ciliary action and causes nuclear vacuolization and fragmentation of tracheal epithelial cells, leading to inflammation and desquamation of the mucosa. Clinically that is a tracheobronchitis with a persistent, minimally productive cough and airway dysfunction.

Massive watery diarrhea with fluid and electrolyte loss: incorrect. Watery diarrhea from fluid loss is caused by cholera toxin.

Spastic paralysis beginning in the masseter muscles: incorrect. Spastic paralysis starting with trismus is caused by tetanus toxin.

A necrotic black skin lesion at the inoculation site: incorrect. A black necrotic eschar is cutaneous anthrax.

Pseudomembrane formation over the tonsils and pharynx: incorrect. A pharyngeal pseudomembrane is produced by diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Persistent cough with inflammation and airway dysfunction: correct. CARDS toxin damages ciliated airway epithelium, producing inflammation, cough, and airway dysfunction.

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old man has 2 days of shaking chills, fever, pleuritic chest pain, and a productive cough. Temperature is 39.1 C (102.4 F). Chest imaging shows consolidation of the right lower lobe. Sputum Gram stain shows lancet-shaped Gram-positive cocci in pairs. On blood agar the isolate is catalase negative and produces partial (alpha) hemolysis, and growth is inhibited around an optochin disk.

Which component of this organism is most responsible for its virulence in this infection?
choices: Polysaccharide capsule
Lipopolysaccharide endotoxin
Protein A on the cell surface
Streptolysin O
Lipoteichoic acid anchoring
questions.note:
**Optochin-sensitive, lancet-shaped alpha-hemolytic diplococci are S. pneumoniae, whose polysaccharide capsule is the essential virulence factor.**

Lancet-shaped, catalase-negative, alpha-hemolytic diplococci that are optochin sensitive are Streptococcus pneumoniae, the most frequent cause of pneumonia and a common cause of otitis media, sinusitis, bacteremia and meningitis.

Its polysaccharide capsule is the essential virulence factor, blocking phagocytosis; the one exception taught here is conjunctivitis, caused by unencapsulated strains. The capsular polysaccharides also form the basis of the two available vaccine types.

Polysaccharide capsule: correct. The polysaccharide capsule is the essential virulence factor of S. pneumoniae.

Lipopolysaccharide endotoxin: incorrect. Lipopolysaccharide is in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, which this is not.

Protein A on the cell surface: incorrect. Protein A is a surface protein of S. aureus.

Streptolysin O: incorrect. Streptolysin O is a hemolysin of S. pyogenes, which is beta hemolytic and bacitracin sensitive.

Lipoteichoic acid anchoring: incorrect. Lipoteichoic acid anchors wall components in Gram-positives generally and is not the key virulence factor here.

questions.stem:
A 2-day-old girl born at 36 weeks becomes lethargic and feeds poorly. Temperature is 38.6 C (101.5 F) and respiratory rate is 72/min. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures grow catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains that produce complete (beta) hemolysis and grow around a bacitracin disk without inhibition.

The infant most likely acquired this organism from which source?
choices: Respiratory droplets from a household contact with strep throat
Skin flora of the nursery staff entering through the umbilical stump
Oral flora introduced into the bloodstream during a feeding
Contaminated soft cheese eaten by the mother during pregnancy
Colonization of the mother's vaginal and gastrointestinal tract
questions.note:
**A bacitracin-resistant beta-hemolytic streptococcus in a septic newborn is group B Streptococcus, acquired from maternal genital and gastrointestinal colonization.**

Beta-hemolytic streptococci split by bacitracin: S. pyogenes (group A) is sensitive and S. agalactiae (group B) is resistant. A bacitracin-resistant beta-hemolytic streptococcus causing sepsis and meningitis in a newborn is group B Streptococcus.

Group B Streptococcus is part of the normal gastrointestinal and urogenital flora, and a sizable fraction of women carry it in the vagina. The newborn acquires it from the mother around delivery, which is why it is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, and meningitis.

**Beta-hemolytic streptococcus | Bacitracin | Classic setting**

- S. pyogenes (group A): Sensitive; Pharyngitis, cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis
- S. agalactiae (group B): Resistant; Neonatal sepsis, pneumonia, meningitis

Respiratory droplets from a household contact with strep throat: incorrect. Strep throat is caused by group A Streptococcus, which is bacitracin sensitive.

Skin flora of the nursery staff entering through the umbilical stump: incorrect. Skin flora suggests staphylococci, which are catalase positive and grow in clusters.

Oral flora introduced into the bloodstream during a feeding: incorrect. Oral viridans streptococci are alpha hemolytic and cause endocarditis, not neonatal sepsis.

Contaminated soft cheese eaten by the mother during pregnancy: incorrect. Soft cheese in pregnancy points to Listeria, a Gram-positive rod that is catalase positive.

Colonization of the mother's vaginal and gastrointestinal tract: correct. Group B Streptococcus colonizes the maternal genital and gastrointestinal tract and is passed to the newborn at birth.

questions.stem:
A 67-year-old man presents with fever and weight loss. Blood cultures grow catalase-negative, oxidase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains that are non-hemolytic and carry the Lancefield group D antigen. In the laboratory the isolate fails to grow in broth containing 6.5% sodium chloride. Echocardiography shows vegetations on two valves.

Which additional evaluation is most important for this patient?
choices: Dental examination for caries and recent extractions
Urine culture for a catheter-associated infection
Colonoscopy to look for a colorectal malignancy
Chest imaging to look for a lobar pneumonia
Echocardiography of the newborn's family members
questions.note:
**Group D streptococci that do not grow in 6.5% NaCl are the S. bovis group, whose bacteremia or endocarditis is associated with colorectal cancer.**

Group D, non-hemolytic, catalase-negative cocci split by salt tolerance: enterococci grow in 6.5% NaCl, while the S. bovis group does not. Failure to grow in high salt identifies the S. bovis group, a gut commensal that causes bacteremia and endocarditis, often on multiple valves.

Fecal carriage of S. bovis group organisms is strongly associated with colorectal cancer, so bacteremia or endocarditis with this organism should prompt a search of the colon.

Dental examination for caries and recent extractions: incorrect. Dental sources fit viridans streptococci, which are alpha hemolytic and lack the group D antigen.

Urine culture for a catheter-associated infection: incorrect. Catheter-associated urinary infection fits enterococci, which grow in 6.5% NaCl.

Colonoscopy to look for a colorectal malignancy: correct. S. bovis group bacteremia is linked to colorectal cancer, so the colon should be examined.

Chest imaging to look for a lobar pneumonia: incorrect. Lobar pneumonia points to S. pneumoniae, an optochin-sensitive alpha-hemolytic diplococcus.

Echocardiography of the newborn's family members: incorrect. Screening family members has no role; S. bovis group is a commensal of the patient's own gut.

questions.stem:
A 72-year-old woman with a long-term indwelling bladder catheter has flank pain and fever. Urine pH is 8.4 and the urine smells strongly of ammonia. Imaging shows a large branching stone filling the renal pelvis. Culture grows a motile, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose, produces hydrogen sulfide, and spreads in waves across the agar surface rather than forming discrete colonies.

Which bacterial enzyme best explains the stone and the urine findings?
choices: Urease
Catalase
Coagulase
Hyaluronidase
Beta-lactamase
questions.note:
**Proteus species are swarming, hydrogen sulfide-producing, urease-positive rods whose urease alkalinizes urine and causes struvite stones.**

A non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod that produces hydrogen sulfide and swarms over the plate is Proteus. P. mirabilis is a leading cause of urinary tract infection after E. coli.

Proteus makes a very potent urease, which splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. The ammonia alkalinizes the urine, giving the high pH and ammoniacal odor, and alkaline urine precipitates struvite, which forms the large branching stones seen here.

Urease: correct. Urease splits urea into ammonia, alkalinizing urine and precipitating struvite stones.

Catalase: incorrect. Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide and does not change urine pH.

Coagulase: incorrect. Coagulase clots plasma and is a marker of S. aureus.

Hyaluronidase: incorrect. Hyaluronidase spreads bacteria through connective tissue and does not alter urine chemistry.

Beta-lactamase: incorrect. Beta-lactamase destroys beta-lactam antibiotics but has no role in stone formation.

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old boy in a refugee camp has 4 days of fever, cramping abdominal pain, painful straining at stool, and frequent small-volume bloody, mucoid stools. He now has pallor and decreased urine output. Laboratory results are shown.

Hemoglobin: 7.9 g/dL (11.5 to 15.5)
Platelets: 48,000/microL (150,000 to 400,000)
Creatinine: 2.6 mg/dL (0.3 to 0.7)

Stool culture grows a non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod that does not produce hydrogen sulfide.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
choices: Campylobacter jejuni
Vibrio cholerae
Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis
Shigella dysenteriae
Yersinia enterocolitica
questions.note:
**Non-motile, hydrogen sulfide-negative Shigella, especially S. dysenteriae, produces Shiga toxin and can cause dysentery complicated by hemolytic uremic syndrome.**

Dysentery (cramps, tenesmus, small-volume bloody mucoid stools) in a crowded setting, with a non-motile, non-lactose-fermenting, hydrogen sulfide-negative Gram-negative rod, points to Shigella. S. dysenteriae is the usual cause of dysentery epidemics in confined populations and is the strongest producer of Shiga toxin.

Shiga toxin damages small blood vessels, especially in the gut and kidney, and can lead to hemolytic uremic syndrome: anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure, exactly the triad in this boy.

Campylobacter jejuni: incorrect. C. jejuni is a comma-shaped microaerophile linked to Guillain-Barre syndrome.

Vibrio cholerae: incorrect. V. cholerae causes profuse watery diarrhea without blood.

Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis: incorrect. Salmonella is motile and produces hydrogen sulfide, giving black colonies on Hektoen agar.

Shigella dysenteriae: correct. S. dysenteriae is non-motile, makes Shiga toxin, and causes dysentery with hemolytic uremic syndrome.

Yersinia enterocolitica: incorrect. Y. enterocolitica causes mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis, usually after undercooked pork.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman returns from 6 weeks visiting family in South Asia. Over 10 days she has had a headache and a fever that climbed in a stepwise fashion to 39.8 C (103.6 F). Pulse is 68/min. Faint pink macules are present on the abdomen, and the liver and spleen are enlarged. She had no diarrhea early in the illness. Blood cultures grow a motile, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that produces hydrogen sulfide.

Which feature of this organism best explains the prolonged systemic illness without early diarrhea?
choices: Invasion of colonic epithelium with intense acute inflammation
Attachment to the gastric mucosa under a urease-generated ammonia cloud
Adherence to fibrin-platelet aggregates on cardiac valves
Production of a toxin that raises intracellular cAMP in enterocytes
Prolonged replication inside macrophages that carry it through the lymphatics
questions.note:
**Salmonella Typhi survives and multiplies within macrophages and disseminates through lymphatics, producing stepwise fever, rose spots and hepatosplenomegaly before any diarrhea.**

A traveler with stepwise fever, a relatively slow pulse, rose spots, hepatosplenomegaly, and a motile hydrogen sulfide-producing Gram-negative rod in blood has typhoid fever from Salmonella Typhi.

Unlike other Salmonella serovars, Typhi inhibits the oxidative burst and keeps replicating inside macrophages rather than killing them. The organisms are carried through the lymphatics to mesenteric nodes, spleen, liver, and bone marrow, producing a mononuclear response with little intestinal irritation, so fever and systemic signs dominate and diarrhea appears only later.

Invasion of colonic epithelium with intense acute inflammation: incorrect. Colonic invasion with acute inflammation describes Shigella dysentery.

Attachment to the gastric mucosa under a urease-generated ammonia cloud: incorrect. Urease and ammonia protection describe Helicobacter pylori in the stomach.

Adherence to fibrin-platelet aggregates on cardiac valves: incorrect. Dextran-mediated adherence to valves describes viridans streptococci.

Production of a toxin that raises intracellular cAMP in enterocytes: incorrect. Raising cAMP in enterocytes is cholera toxin, which causes watery diarrhea, not prolonged fever.

Prolonged replication inside macrophages that carry it through the lymphatics: correct. Salmonella Typhi replicates within macrophages and spreads through lymphatics, producing systemic illness before diarrhea.

questions.stem:
A 63-year-old smoker staying at a large hotel develops myalgia and headache, then high fever, a dry cough, pleuritic chest pain, diarrhea, and confusion over 4 days. Chest imaging shows patchy infiltrates. Sputum is scant, and a Gram stain of respiratory secretions shows many neutrophils but essentially no organisms. Routine blood agar cultures show no growth after 48 hours.

Growth of this organism in the laboratory most requires which condition?
choices: Chocolate agar supplemented with factors V and X
Medium enriched with L-cysteine and iron
A cell culture monolayer, since it cannot grow on agar
Anaerobic incubation for 4 to 10 days
Medium containing 6.5% sodium chloride
questions.note:
**Legionella pneumophila stains poorly and fails to grow on blood agar; it requires L-cysteine and iron, supplied by buffered charcoal yeast extract agar.**

A severe pneumonia with prominent systemic features (high fever, diarrhea, confusion) acquired in a large building with a cooling tower, where the Gram stain shows neutrophils without visible organisms, is Legionnaires disease. Legionella stains poorly because of its unusual, highly hydrophobic lipopolysaccharide, so silver impregnation methods are used instead.

Legionella will not grow on common media such as blood agar. It needs L-cysteine, iron and slightly acidic conditions, supplied by buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, and growth takes 2 to 5 days.

Chocolate agar supplemented with factors V and X: incorrect. Factors V and X on chocolate agar are the requirements of Haemophilus influenzae.

Medium enriched with L-cysteine and iron: correct. Legionella needs L-cysteine and iron, provided by buffered charcoal yeast extract agar.

A cell culture monolayer, since it cannot grow on agar: incorrect. Legionella is a facultative intracellular organism but does grow on the proper agar; Chlamydia is the one that needs host cells.

Anaerobic incubation for 4 to 10 days: incorrect. Legionella is aerobic, not anaerobic.

Medium containing 6.5% sodium chloride: incorrect. High salt medium is used to test enterococci.

questions.stem:
A 19-year-old college student has 10 days of low-grade fever, headache, malaise, sore throat, earache, and a dry cough. He looks well enough to attend classes. Chest imaging shows patchy infiltrates in one lower lobe out of proportion to how well he appears. He was given amoxicillin 5 days ago with no improvement. Cultures of respiratory secretions eventually grow colonies with a fried-egg appearance.

Which structural feature of this organism best explains the failure of the initial antibiotic?
choices: A waxy mycolic acid outer layer
An outer membrane with low-permeability porins
A polysaccharide capsule that blocks drug binding
Absence of a peptidoglycan cell wall
Efflux pumps that expel beta-lactam drugs
questions.note:
**Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall and uses host cholesterol in its membrane, so beta-lactams are ineffective.**

Walking pneumonia in a young adult with headache, sore throat, earache, a dry cough, and fried-egg colonies in culture is Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Its radiographic findings are typically worse than the patient appears.

Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan cell wall. Its membrane is reinforced with sterols including cholesterol taken from the host instead. Since beta-lactams act on cell wall synthesis, they cannot work here, and the preferred agents are doxycycline or azithromycin.

A waxy mycolic acid outer layer: incorrect. Mycolic acids are the waxy barrier of mycobacteria and Nocardia.

An outer membrane with low-permeability porins: incorrect. Low-permeability porins describe Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

A polysaccharide capsule that blocks drug binding: incorrect. A capsule does not prevent beta-lactams from reaching penicillin-binding proteins.

Absence of a peptidoglycan cell wall: correct. Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan cell wall, so cell wall-active drugs are useless.

Efflux pumps that expel beta-lactam drugs: incorrect. Efflux pumps contribute to resistance in other organisms but are not why Mycoplasma resists beta-lactams.

questions.stem:
A 21-year-old woman has 2 weeks of sore throat and hoarseness followed by a cough that persists, with low-grade fever, congestion, fatigue, and headache. Chest imaging shows a mild infiltrate. A Gram stain of respiratory secretions shows no organisms, and the laboratory notes that the agent was recovered only in cell culture, where it formed inclusions within epithelial cells.

Which property of this organism best explains why it cannot be grown on standard agar?
choices: It grows only at temperatures above 42 degrees Celsius
It requires L-cysteine and iron that agar lacks
It depends on host cells for amino acids and ATP
It forms spores that remain dormant on artificial media
It is killed by the oxygen tension at an agar surface
questions.note:
**Chlamydophila pneumoniae is an obligate intracellular parasite dependent on host amino acids and ATP, so it cannot be cultured on cell-free media.**

A young adult with pharyngitis or laryngitis weeks before a lingering cough and a mild atypical pneumonia, with an agent that stains poorly and forms intracellular inclusions, has Chlamydophila pneumoniae. It lacks peptidoglycan, so it does not take the Gram stain well.

Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular parasites because they rely on the host cell for key amino acids and for energy-generating metabolites such as ATP. That dependence, not a nutrient that could simply be added to agar, is why they grow only inside cells.

It grows only at temperatures above 42 degrees Celsius: incorrect. Growth at 42 degrees is a feature used to identify Campylobacter jejuni.

It requires L-cysteine and iron that agar lacks: incorrect. L-cysteine and iron are the special needs of Legionella, which does grow on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar.

It depends on host cells for amino acids and ATP: correct. Chlamydiae depend on host cells for amino acids and ATP, so they require living cells to grow.

It forms spores that remain dormant on artificial media: incorrect. Chlamydiae do not form spores; spore formers include Bacillus and Clostridioides.

It is killed by the oxygen tension at an agar surface: incorrect. Oxygen tension is not the limiting factor; Chlamydophila pneumoniae is aerobic.

questions.stem:
A 7-year-old girl has a sore throat, fever, and a diffuse sandpaper-like rash with a red, bumpy tongue. A throat swab grows catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains that produce complete (beta) hemolysis and are inhibited by a bacitracin disk. Blood tests show a markedly elevated white blood cell count with many activated T cells.

The rash and the widespread T cell activation are best explained by which bacterial product?
choices: An enterotoxin that forms pores in epithelial cells
Pyrogenic exotoxins that act as superantigens
An A-B toxin that blocks neurotransmitter release
A urease that generates ammonia in tissue
A protease that cleaves immunoglobulin A only
questions.note:
**Streptococcus pyogenes pyrogenic exotoxins (SpeA, SpeB, SpeC) cause the scarlet fever rash and act as superantigens driving nonspecific T cell activation.**

Pharyngitis with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue in a child, caused by a bacitracin-sensitive, beta-hemolytic chain-forming coccus, is scarlet fever from Streptococcus pyogenes.

Most strains make streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins. SpeA and SpeC are also called erythrogenic toxins and produce the rash, and SpeA and SpeB act as superantigens, cross-linking many T cell receptors nonspecifically and driving the fever and massive T cell activation that can progress to toxic shock syndrome.

An enterotoxin that forms pores in epithelial cells: incorrect. Pore-forming enterotoxins describe the B. cereus diarrheal toxin, not scarlet fever.

Pyrogenic exotoxins that act as superantigens: correct. Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens and cause the scarlet fever rash.

An A-B toxin that blocks neurotransmitter release: incorrect. Blocking neurotransmitter release describes tetanus and botulinum toxins.

A urease that generates ammonia in tissue: incorrect. Urease belongs to Proteus and Helicobacter.

A protease that cleaves immunoglobulin A only: incorrect. An immunoglobulin A protease alone does not produce rash or superantigen activity.

questions.stem:
Three patients present with community-acquired pneumonia. Patient 1 is a 20-year-old with sore throat, earache, headache, and a dry cough for 3 weeks who remains ambulatory. Patient 2 is a 70-year-old who became confused and had diarrhea and high fever over 4 days after staying in a hotel with a cooling tower. Patient 3 is a 22-year-old with hoarseness and a sore throat 2 weeks before a mild cough and infiltrate. All three have respiratory specimens whose Gram stains show no organisms.

Which assignment of organisms to patients is correct?
choices: 1 Legionella, 2 Mycoplasma, 3 Chlamydophila
1 Chlamydophila, 2 Mycoplasma, 3 Legionella
1 Mycoplasma, 2 Legionella, 3 Chlamydophila
1 Mycoplasma, 2 Chlamydophila, 3 Legionella
1 Legionella, 2 Chlamydophila, 3 Mycoplasma
questions.note:
**The three atypical pneumonia agents are separated clinically: Mycoplasma causes walking pneumonia, Legionella a severe water-associated pneumonia with diarrhea and confusion, and Chlamydophila a mild illness preceded by pharyngitis.**

All three atypical agents fail to appear on Gram stain, so the clinical pattern decides. A young ambulatory patient with earache, headache and a dry cough lasting weeks is Mycoplasma pneumoniae, the walking pneumonia.

An older patient with high fever, diarrhea and confusion after exposure to aerosols from a building water system has Legionnaires disease, the severe form of atypical pneumonia. Pharyngitis or laryngitis one to three weeks before a mild lower respiratory illness is the pattern of Chlamydophila pneumoniae.

**Agent | Clue | Laboratory**

- Mycoplasma pneumoniae: Young, ambulatory, earache, dry cough; Fried-egg colonies, no cell wall
- Legionella pneumophila: Water aerosols, diarrhea, confusion; Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar, silver stain
- Chlamydophila pneumoniae: Pharyngitis or laryngitis then cough; Obligate intracellular, inclusions

1 Legionella, 2 Mycoplasma, 3 Chlamydophila: incorrect. Legionella does not present as a mild ambulatory illness in a young adult.

1 Chlamydophila, 2 Mycoplasma, 3 Legionella: incorrect. Chlamydophila does not cause the severe confusion and diarrhea seen in patient 2.

1 Mycoplasma, 2 Legionella, 3 Chlamydophila: correct. Walking pneumonia is Mycoplasma, the severe water-aerosol case is Legionella, and preceding laryngitis is Chlamydophila.
